:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Given the system


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3y &=4 \\ -4x+6y &=-8,\end{aligned}\right.
$$


which of the following statements are true?

- The system is consistent dependent

- The system has no solution

- The system is consistent independent
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is


$$
M= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -3 & 4 \\ -4 & 6 & -8\end{array} \right].
$$



Using Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 4 \\ -4 & 6 & -8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3y &=4 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Since any numbers $x$ and $y$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
2x -3y= 4
$$

The basic variable is $x,$ and we have a free variable $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, since there are infinitely many solutions, we conclude that the system is *consistent dependent*.

As a result, only statement I is true.

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 6 \\ 2 & -3 & 13 \\ 5 & -1 & 45\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 6 \\ 2 & -3 & 13 \\ 5 & -1 & 45\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 25 \\ 5 & -1 & 45\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 25 \\ 0 & 9 & 75\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-9){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & 25 \\ 0 & 0 & -150\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the following system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+3y &=-1 \\ x-2y &=1 \\ -x-5y &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
To classify the system, we first try to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & -3 \\ -1 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & -7 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since any numbers $x$ and $y$ are solutions to the third equation $0x+0y=0$, we can remove this equation from the system. So, the corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=1 \\ 7y &=-3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $y=-\frac{3}{7}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2\left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)=1\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{7}.
$$

 
So, we conclude that the system is consistent independent. 

As a result, only statement “The system is consistent independent” is true.

\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & -3 \\ -6 & -4 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y &=-3 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any numbers $x$ and $y$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
3x+2y=-3
$$

The basic variable is $x,$ and we have a free variable $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, since there are infinitely many solutions, we conclude that the system is *consistent dependent*.

As a result, only statement II is true.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+5y+z &=2 \\ x+5y+2z &=5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$


Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is


$$
M= \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 5 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 5 & 2 & 5\end{array} \right].
$$



Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 5 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+5y &=-1 \\ z &=3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $z,$ and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $z$ in terms of $y.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-1-5y \\ y &=y \\ z &=3,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1-5y \\ y \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Determine the value of $k$ for which the following system of linear equations is inconsistent:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-2y &=1, \\ 4x+ky &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is



$$
M= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & k & -3\end{array} \right].
$$



Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & k & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & k+4 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now 



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-2y &=1 \\ (k+4)y &=-5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



The system is inconsistent if it has no solutions. For the system to have no solutions, one of the equations above must be false.

If $k=-4,$ then the second equation is $0=-5,$ which is false, and the system will have no solution.

Therefore, our system is inconsistent when $k=-4.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We can use Gaussian elimination to find the general solutions of systems with any number of equations and variables. For instance, consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1, \\ y+3z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system has the augmented matrix


$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0\end{array}\right].
$$



Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\, & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+4z &=1 \\ y+3z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We see that the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable $z.$ From the second equation, we get $y=-3z,$ and from the first equation, we obtain $x=1-4z.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1-4z, \\ y &=-3z, \\ z &=z.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1-4z \\ -3z \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+z\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Recall that a system of linear equations is called **consistent** if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, if there are no solutions, the system is called **inconsistent**. 

For a consistent system, 

- the system is called **consistent independent** if the solution is unique, while

- the system is called **consistent dependent** if there are infinitely many solutions.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Show that the following system of equations has no solution.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x + 2y &=4 \\ 2x + y &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's start by solving the system using elimination.

Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-2$, then we will get a $-4x$ term that can cancel with the $4x$ term in the first equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y &=4 \\ 2x+y &=4 && \text{multiply by } -2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a false statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x + 2y &= 4 \\
- 4x - 2y &= -8 \\
0 &= (4 - 8) \\
0 &= -4
\end{aligned}
$$

The statement $0=-4$ is *always false*. Therefore, we conclude that the system has *no solutions*.

Geometrically, this means that the corresponding lines *do not intersect*. In other words, they are *parallel.*

![](images/04/048c377f99093f493c37bc4de0363527996c8928348b43ad9c9747965f984c1f.png)

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
At how many points do the following lines intersect?

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y &= 2 \\[6pt]
10y - 5x &= -10
\end{aligned}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The number of points of intersection between the two lines is equal to the number of solutions of the corresponding system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x - 2y &=2 \\ 10y - 5x &=-10\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve the system using substitution. First, we solve for $x$ in the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y &= 2 \\
x &= 2y + 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute

$$
x=2y+2
$$

into the second equation and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
10y - 5x &= -10 \\
10y - 5(2y + 2) &= -10 \\
10y - 10y - 10 &= -10 \\
- 10 &= -10
\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a statement that's always true. Therefore, we conclude that the system has infinitely many solutions.

Consequently, the lines intersect at infinitely many points (i.e., they coincide).

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Number of Intersection Points of Two Lines

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find all points of intersection of the following lines:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x+2y &= 2 \\[6pt]
6x+4y &= 4
\end{aligned}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The points of intersection of the lines correspond to the solutions of the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x + 2y &=2 \\ 6x + 4y &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve the system using elimination. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$, then we will get a $-6x$ term that can cancel with the $6x$ term in the second equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y &=2 && \text{multiply by } -2 \\ 6x+4y &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-6x - 4y &= -4 \\
6x + 4y &= 4 \\
0 &= (-4 + 4) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the lines have infinitely many intersection points.

We want to find an expression that represents every solution to the system. Any value of $x$ is a solution, and we can find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the lines for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x + 2y &= 2 \\
2y &= 2 - 3x \\
y &= \frac{2 - 3x}{2} \\
y &= 1 - \frac{3}{2}x
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points of intersection are

$$
\left(x,1-\dfrac{3}{2}x \right)
$$

where $x$ is any number.

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the General Solution to a System With Infinitely Many Intersection Points
